articles.title: Transcranial Focused Ultrasound: A Transformative Tool for Intracranial Ablation, Drug Delivery, and Neuromodulation
articles.content: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) is an emerging neuromodulation and therapeutic technology offering noninvasive, submillimeter precision for targeting deep brain structures. Unlike transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial electric stimulation (tES), which are limited by depth-focality tradeoffs, or deep brain stimulation (DBS), which is invasive and costly, tFUS enables precise modulation with minimal risk. Its applications include ablation for movement and psychiatric disorders, blood-brain barrier opening (BBBO) for drug delivery in neuro-oncology and neurodegeneration, and neuromodulation for circuit-based interventions in addiction, mood/anxiety disorders, and chronic pain. Advances in phased-array transducers, holographic focusing, and real-time imaging continue to refine its accuracy and safety. Ongoing research explores closed-loop systems and wearable devices to expand clinical accessibility. This review outlines the physics, current applications, and future directions of tFUS, positioning it as a transformative tool in personalized neuromodulation and neurotherapeutics.

articles.title: Network Models of Neurodegeneration: Bridging Neuronal Dynamics and Disease Progression
articles.content: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by the accumulation of misfolded proteins and widespread disruptions in brain function. Computational modeling has advanced our understanding of these processes, but efforts have traditionally focused on either neuronal dynamics or the biological processes underlying disease. One class of models uses neural mass and whole-brain frameworks to simulate changes in oscillations, connectivity, and network stability. A second class focuses on biological processes underlying disease progression, particularly prion-like propagation through the connectome, glial responses and vascular mechanisms. Each modeling tradition has provided important insights, but experimental evidence shows these processes are interconnected: neuronal activity modulates protein release and clearance, while pathological burden disrupts neuronal function. Modeling these domains in isolation limits our understanding, although recent studies have begun to bridge the two by coupling neuronal and pathological processes. To determine where and why disease emerges, how it spreads, and how it might be altered, mathematical models that capture feedback between neuronal dynamics and disease biology are needed. This review surveys the two modeling approaches and highlights efforts to unify them, emphasizing that linking neuronal activity and disease progression is key to identifying strategies that slow, halt, or reverse degeneration and restore neural function.

articles.title: Optogenetics: Pinpoint Light on Precise Neuromodulation
articles.content: Optogenetics has emerged as a pivotal tool in neuroscience, enabling intricate modulation of targeted neurons within the nervous system. Despite its transformative potential, achieving high spatiotemporal resolution in neuromodulation remains a significant challenge, particularly in free-behaving animals. This review aims to highlight recent advances in optogenetic systems for neuromodulation, focusing on the efforts to achieve superior precision in spatiotemporal control. We provide a comprehensive overview of the breakthroughs in optogenetic tools that offer ultrafast responsiveness, strategies for targeted tissue- and cell-specific optogene delivery, and methods for precise optical stimulation with minimal impact on the behavior of subjects. Additionally, we review the applications of optogenetics in neurological diseases, emphasizing its potential to advance therapeutic interventions. These innovations are poised to propel optogenetics into a new era, accelerating its clinical translation for precision neuromodulation and treatment of neurological disorders.

articles.title: Emerging Noninvasive Approaches for the Suppression of Pathological Tremor
articles.content: Pathological tremor affects over 40 million people worldwide, significantly impairing daily activities and quality of life. Pharmacological treatments show limited efficacy, with up to 30% discontinuation rates, while surgical interventions like deep brain stimulation achieve significant tremor reduction but are often unsuitable due to age, comorbidities, or personal preference. Recently, the need for safe and effective alternatives has led to the development of innovative, noninvasive, and patient-friendly technologies for tremor management. This clinical application review analyzed 134 studies (1969-2025), categorizing them into three major modalities, focusing on their underlying neurophysiological mechanisms, with a special emphasis on the clinical perspective. The three considered modalities were force-controlling (orthoses and functional electrical stimulation), central neuromodulation (transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial electrical stimulation, low-intensity focused ultrasound, and transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation), and peripheral neuromodulation (afferent stimulation and vibration). Force-controlling strategies showed promising acute effects, though clinical translation remains limited by poor wearability and the development of muscle fatigue. Central neuromodulation produced moderate effects, while peripheral neuromodulation has gained clinical traction, with several devices now being commercially available. However, heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, and technology maturity remain the main obstacles for the direct comparison of techniques. Future research should prioritize larger multicenter trials, standardized outcome measures, and accessibility considerations to enable personalized, evidence-based treatment selection for diverse tremor populations.

articles.title: Assistive Trajectory Planning for Lower Limb Exoskeletons: Strategies From Laboratory-Optimized Gait to Environmentally-Adaptive Locomotion Through Multimodal Parameter Awareness
articles.content: Lower limb assistive exoskeletons (LLEs) show great potential to reduce metabolic cost, improve walking performance, and correct abnormal gait patterns. Among their core control architectures, assistive trajectory planning is key to determining system responsiveness and effectiveness under varying locomotion conditions. Many trajectory planning methods were proposed in either laboratory or unstructured real-world environments. To clarify the scope and challenges of existing research, this review categorizes trajectory planning strategies into two major types based on application scenarios: (1) strategies for laboratory settings with controllable disturbances, which usually involve optimal control for gait under stable or controllable conditions; and (2) strategies for real-world environments characterized by varying terrain, individual differences, and gait fluctuations, which usually involve adaptive control for gait under diverse or unstructured conditions. Given the foundational role of gait phase detection in trajectory planning, this review also systematically examines mainstream algorithms for gait phase recognition and estimation. Finally, the paper analyzes the limitations of existing methods and discusses the potential of advanced algorithms, intelligent multimodal sensing systems, novel sensing technologies, and embedded deployment to enhance the performance of exoskeleton assistive trajectory planning.

articles.title: Dynamical disorders: synchronization dynamics in complex emotional conditions
articles.content: IntroductionMental health conditions present a particular challenge to categorical nosology. We propose that such conditions are better understood as Dynamical Disorders, defined not only by symptom cluster profiles but by underlying disrupted patterns of coordination across bio-psycho-social scales. We present an exemplary case study of Complex Emotional Needs (CEN) presentations. Its transdiagnostic scope, process-defined clinical presentation, and 40–60% non-remission rates under current protocols reflect a mismatch between categorical nosology and the dynamic, multi-scale psycho-neurobiological processes underlying these conditions.MethodsDrawing on affective neuroscience and synchronization dynamics, we propose reconceptualizing CEN as disorders of flexible functional synchronization across nested bio-psycho-social scales.ResultsWe derive four dynamical phenotypes from the parameter space governing multi-scale synchronization and specify how to operationalize them empirically. They exhibit characteristic dynamical-landscape topologies, quantified by basin curvature, energy barrier heights, and stability exponents. Simulations of the master equation generate dynamical landscape topologies and phenotype-specific parameter regimes.DiscussionThis approach yields pragmatic, testable predictions of clinical dynamics and corresponding treatments. We consider the algorithmic selection of phenotype-matched modular interventions targeting specific coordination failures, along with a validation program that AI agents can eventually augment. We present falsifiable predictions for comparative trials between phenotype-matched and treatment-as-usual approaches. This framework offers a principled path toward evidence-based mental health care grounded in human synchronization dynamics.
articles.author: S. S. Høgenhaug

articles.title: Epigenetic modification of neurotransmitter pathways during fasting: a systematic review
articles.content: BackgroundDietary restriction, encompassing intermittent fasting and caloric restriction, represents a prominent non-pharmacological approach to modulating brain aging and neuronal resilience. Emerging evidence links metabolism to long-term neural plasticity through epigenetic mechanisms, yet findings remain fragmented. This review integrates preclinical evidence on how dietary restriction alters brain epigenetic regulation and links these changes to neurocognitive outcomes.MethodsThe review followed PRISMA 2020 and the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline. PubMed and SciSpace were searched from inception to December 2025. Eligible studies assessed DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNA, or epigenetic regulators in brain tissue of animal or human subjects undergoing dietary restriction. Risk of bias was appraised with the SYRCLE tool, and a qualitative narrative synthesis was undertaken given methodological heterogeneity.ResultsNine preclinical animal studies met the inclusion criteria; no human study qualified. Dietary restriction significantly affected DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA expression, exerting a recalibrating influence that attenuated age-associated epigenetic drift and restored homeostatic regulation. Sirtuin-1/CREB signalling, BDNF/TrkB signalling, metabolic signalling (mTOR, AMPK, FOXO), and neuroinflammatory modulation were the principal pathways implicated. Intermittent fasting and caloric restriction showed overlapping and distinct mechanisms, with ketone-induced histone deacetylase inhibition linked to fasting. Cognitive benefit, particularly in hippocampal-dependent memory, accompanied the epigenetic changes, although persistent epigenetic memory of dietary restriction was less clear. Risk of bias was high in seven studies and moderate in two, reflecting incomplete reporting of randomisation, blinding, and protocols.ConclusionDietary restriction alters brain epigenetics through multiple interconnected pathways that strengthen neural circuits and improve cognitive function. The preclinical evidence is consistent across several layers of epigenetic regulation, but the absence of human studies, small sample sizes, and limited causal evidence constrain translation. Multi-omics approaches and epigenome editing are required to establish causality and the therapeutic potential of dietary restriction.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420251035303.

articles.title: Path planning algorithm based on pulse-coupled neural network with dual constraints of heading-deviation and node penalty
articles.content: Path planning for mobile robots is a crucial aspect of robot navigation. Traditional search algorithms are limited by heuristic design and search strategies, often struggling to balance search efficiency and path quality in intricate obstacle environments. The Pulse-Coupled Neural Network (PCNN) offers inherent parallelism and completeness due to its autowave propagation mechanism. Nevertheless, the lack of directional guidance in the neuron activation process necessitates the activation of a significant number of free grid cells on extensive maps, thereby impeding search efficiency. This paper introduces a Dual-Constrained PCNN path planning algorithm to tackle the aforementioned issues. The algorithm incorporates two constraint mechanisms within the PCNN autowave propagation framework. The first mechanism involves a penalty term for heading deviation, which adjusts the internal activity of neurons based on the angle deviation between the current and target directions. This adjustment facilitates the autowave propagation toward the desired direction. The second mechanism involves a node penalty term that adjusts the dynamic threshold of neurons, which guides the path to converge precisely toward the goal. By synergistically integrating these two constraints, the algorithm effectively reduces redundant activation, improves the PCNN autowave propagation process, and ultimately enhances planning efficiency. To assess the proposed method’s generalization ability across diverse environments, a comprehensive experimental setup was devised, encompassing varied map dimensions, obstacle densities, and obstacle configurations. Results indicate that in environments with sparse obstacles, DC-PCNN demonstrates consistent search success rates across maps of different sizes, with path-planning runtime increasing linearly with map dimensions. The resulting path closely aligns with the straight-line distance between the start and goal points, featuring minimal turns and smooth trajectory, underscoring its robust cross-scale generalization and search efficiency. Conversely, in high-density obstacle settings, the fixed-parameter DC-PCNN exhibits a reduced success rate attributed to excessive directional bias, leading to local entrapment and goal failure. Upon implementing a parameter adaptive strategy, the method’s success rate in high-density scenarios significantly improves, affirming the efficacy of the adaptive mechanism.
articles.author: Xiaoyan Wang

articles.title: Research progress and prospects of cochlear implant technology
articles.content: Traditional cochlear implant systems depend on external devices and face challenges related to convenience, esthetics, and auditory performance in complex soundscapes. Recently, research has shifted from “functional substitution” to “functional enhancement” and “biological fusion.” However, most emerging approaches remain in the preclinical, prototype verification, or early clinical stages, lacking substantial evidence of clinical benefits. This narrative review examines research progress across five key dimensions of cochlear implants: The electrode interface has advanced from passive implants to dynamic, adaptive, and biologically active intelligent interfaces. Signal processing strategies are moving toward intelligence and physiological adaptation, with deep learning primarily used for noise suppression and coding optimization; however, clinical application is limited by real-time performance and individual variability. Bionic sensing aims to replicate the energy conversion mechanism between hair cells and the basement membrane at the signal source, currently focusing on laboratory prototypes. Optogenetics-driven optical regulation offers high spatial selectivity but remains in the early preclinical stage. The development of fully implanted systems emphasizes internal energy supply, ultra-low power consumption processing, and system integration, marking a significant engineering direction for making devices “invisible.” Each section of this article critically evaluates evidence maturity and transformation barriers, highlighting common challenges such as long-term biological stability, safety, energy consumption, and regulatory verification that must be addressed before large-scale clinical application. Future advancements will require collaboration among materials science, neuroscience, microelectronics, and artificial intelligence to create a two-way high-fidelity interface. The ultimate goal is not only to restore hearing but also to reconstruct a more natural auditory perception.
